metadata.description: Narrative templates for milestone→outcome correlations. Used by the app to dynamically generate the 'Does Timing Matter?' section for any country pair.

groups.causal: Plausible causal path from milestone to outcome
groups.common_cause: A third factor (development, policy, wealth) drives both
groups.feedback: Bidirectional reinforcement, both cause each other
groups.artifact: Likely driven by small N, noisy data, or outlier countries

correlations.template: In {high_country}, women marry at {high_val}, and gender inequality is among the lowest in the world ({high_outcome}). In {low_country}, women marry at {low_val}, and inequality remains high ({low_outcome}). When women marry later, they have more years to build education, careers, and economic independence before entering partnerships.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage → more equality
correlations.mechanism: Later marriage gives women more years to build autonomy before domestic obligations. Early marriage often removes women from education and the labor force entirely.
correlations.improvement_path: To reduce gender inequality: Invest in girls' education + remove legal barriers to property/employment → women marry later → build economic independence → inequality shrinks.

correlations.template: In {low_country}, where women marry at {low_val}, maternal mortality is {low_outcome} per 100,000 births. In {high_country}, where they marry at {high_val}, it drops to {high_outcome}. Later marriage means later first pregnancy, and pregnancies after age 25 carry significantly lower medical risk.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage → safer pregnancies
correlations.mechanism: Later marriage delays first pregnancy past the high-risk teenage years. Also correlates with better healthcare access and family planning.
correlations.improvement_path: To reduce maternal deaths: Delay marriage → delay first pregnancy past high-risk teen years + better educated mothers seek prenatal care → fewer complications.

correlations.template: {high_country} marries at {high_val} and lives to {high_outcome}. {low_country} marries at {low_val} and lives to {low_outcome}. Later marriage correlates with longer lives, but longer-lived societies also tend to be ones where people have the freedom to delay marriage.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage ↔ longer lives
correlations.mechanism: Bidirectional: later marriage reduces early-pregnancy risks and allows more resource accumulation. But societies with longer lifespans are also wealthier and more permissive of delayed marriage.
correlations.improvement_path: To extend life expectancy: Later marriage → later first pregnancy (safer) + higher income → better healthcare access → longer lives.

correlations.template: {high_country} marries at {high_val} and stays healthy until {high_outcome}. {low_country} marries at {low_val} and healthy life ends at {low_outcome}. Countries where people marry later tend to have longer healthy lifespans, a gap of {gap} healthy years.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage ↔ more healthy years
correlations.mechanism: Similar to life expectancy: later marriage tracks with better health systems, higher income, and fewer early-pregnancy complications. Reinforcing cycle.
correlations.improvement_path: To increase healthy years: Later marriage → higher income → better nutrition, healthcare, and less poverty-related stress → more years lived in good health.

correlations.template: {high_country} marries at {high_val} with GDP of ${high_outcome}. {low_country} marries at {low_val} with GDP of ${low_outcome}. More productive working years before marriage contributes to higher output, but wealthier economies also reduce the economic pressure to marry early.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage ↔ higher GDP
correlations.mechanism: Both directions: delayed marriage means more working/earning years, boosting GDP. But higher GDP means less economic pressure to form households early.
correlations.improvement_path: To raise GDP: Increase education access for women → delays marriage → more working years → higher economic output per person.

correlations.template: {high_country} marries at {high_val} and scores {high_outcome} on happiness. {low_country} marries at {low_val} and scores {low_outcome}. The freedom to choose when to marry, without economic or social pressure, is itself part of what makes a society happier.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage ↔ more happiness
correlations.mechanism: Societies that allow delayed marriage tend to offer more personal freedom, stronger safety nets, and less social coercion, all of which independently drive happiness.
correlations.improvement_path: To increase happiness: Expand social safety nets → remove pressure to marry for economic survival → people marry by choice → reported happiness rises.

correlations.template: In {high_country}, women marry at {high_val} and {high_outcome}% participate in the workforce. In {low_country}, women marry at {low_val} and only {low_outcome}% do. Every year of delayed marriage is another year women spend building careers instead of exiting the labor force.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage → more women working
correlations.mechanism: Later marriage gives women more time to enter and establish careers. In many countries, marriage (especially early marriage) is the primary exit point from the labor force for women.
correlations.improvement_path: To get more women working: Delay marriage age → more years in education and early career → women establish economic roles before domestic obligations.

correlations.template: Where women marry young, teen pregnancies follow. {low_country} marries at {low_val} and has {low_outcome} adolescent births per 1,000. {high_country} marries at {high_val}, just {high_outcome}.
correlations.one_liner: Earlier marriage → more teen pregnancies
correlations.mechanism: Early marriage directly leads to early pregnancy. Access to contraception, education continuation, and cultural norms around marriage age all mediate this.
correlations.improvement_path: To cut teen pregnancies: Keep girls in school longer → delays marriage → delays first sexual activity → combines with contraceptive access to slash teen births.

correlations.template: {low_country} marries at {low_val} with a fertility rate of {low_outcome}. {high_country} marries at {high_val} with {high_outcome}. Later marriage compresses the window for having children, but the relationship is complicated. Some late-marrying countries (France, Sweden) maintain moderate fertility through policy support.
correlations.one_liner: Later marriage → fewer children (usually)
correlations.mechanism: Delayed marriage shortens the reproductive window within partnership. But strong parental leave and childcare policies can partially offset this compression.

correlations.template: In {high_country}, education ends at {high_val} and {high_outcome}% of women work. In {low_country}, education ends at {low_val} and only {low_outcome}% do. Longer education builds human capital, the skills that make women employable and economically independent.
correlations.one_liner: More education → more women working
correlations.mechanism: Direct human capital effect: longer education produces higher-skilled workers who are more likely to enter and stay in the workforce. One of the most studied relationships in development economics.
correlations.improvement_path: To boost female workforce: More years in education → women gain skills and credentials → enter professional jobs → stay in workforce through marriage and parenthood.

correlations.template: {high_country} finishes education at {high_val} and scores {high_outcome} on happiness. {low_country} finishes at {low_val} and scores {low_outcome}. Education builds both economic opportunity and personal agency, but happier, wealthier societies also invest more in their education systems.
correlations.one_liner: More education ↔ more happiness
correlations.mechanism: Education improves income, health literacy, and agency. But the cycle is reinforcing: happier societies fund better education, which produces happier citizens.
correlations.improvement_path: To increase well-being: Longer education → better jobs → higher income + more social connections + sense of agency → all three are top happiness predictors.

correlations.template: {high_country} keeps students in school until {high_val} and has a GII of {high_outcome}. {low_country} finishes at {low_val} with a GII of {low_outcome}. Education, especially female education, is one of the strongest predictors of gender equality anywhere in the world.
correlations.one_liner: More education → more equality
correlations.mechanism: Education gives women economic independence, political voice, and reproductive autonomy. Countries that educate women longer consistently score better on every gender equality measure.
correlations.improvement_path: To reduce inequality: Educate women longer → they enter professions, earn independently, gain political voice → institutions adapt → inequality falls.

correlations.template: {high_country} educates until {high_val} with GDP of ${high_outcome}. {low_country} until {low_val} with ${low_outcome}. More education produces a more productive economy, but richer countries can also afford to keep people in school longer.
correlations.one_liner: More education ↔ higher GDP
correlations.mechanism: Bidirectional: education builds human capital and productivity, raising GDP. Higher GDP funds longer education. A virtuous cycle when it works, a poverty trap when it doesn't.
correlations.improvement_path: To grow GDP: Extend education by 1 year → each additional year of schooling raises earnings 8-13% → compounds across the workforce → GDP rises.

correlations.template: {high_country} finishes education at {high_val} and lives to {high_outcome}. {low_country} finishes at {low_val} and lives to {low_outcome}. Both are driven by national development, the same investments that build schools also build hospitals.
correlations.one_liner: More education ↔ longer life (development drives both)
correlations.mechanism: National development level drives both: wealthier countries invest in education AND healthcare. Education also has a direct health literacy effect, but the dominant driver is shared investment capacity.
correlations.improvement_path: To extend lifespan: More education → health literacy + higher income → better nutrition, less smoking, more preventive care → 2-3 years longer life per degree.

correlations.template: Where education is longer, fewer mothers die. {high_country} educates until {high_val}, maternal mortality is {high_outcome}. {low_country} until {low_val}, mortality is {low_outcome}. Educated women have more access to prenatal care, family planning, and safer delivery options.
correlations.one_liner: More education → fewer maternal deaths
correlations.mechanism: Education delays childbearing (reducing high-risk teen pregnancies), increases health literacy, and correlates with better healthcare access. Both direct and indirect effects.
correlations.improvement_path: To reduce maternal deaths: Educated women → seek prenatal care, deliver in hospitals, space pregnancies → mortality drops dramatically.

correlations.template: {high_country} finishes education at {high_val} and stays healthy until {high_outcome}. {low_country} finishes at {low_val}, healthy until {low_outcome}. Education and healthy lifespan are both products of a society that invests in its people.
correlations.one_liner: More education → more healthy years (development drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Shared driver: national investment in human capital produces both longer education and better health outcomes. Education also has direct effects on health behavior.

correlations.template: Menopause at {high_val} in {high_country} where {high_outcome}% of women work. Menopause at {low_val} in {low_country} where {low_outcome}% work. These aren't directly connected, both reflect a country's nutrition, healthcare, and opportunities for women.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ more women working (health drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Not causal. Better nutrition and healthcare delay menopause. The same development conditions that produce better health also produce more economic opportunity for women.

correlations.template: Menopause age tracks wealth, {high_val} in {high_country} (GDP ${high_outcome}), {low_val} in {low_country} (GDP ${low_outcome}). This isn't because later menopause creates wealth. It's because the same nutrition and healthcare that delay menopause are products of a wealthier society.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ higher GDP (wealth drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Pure common cause. GDP enables better nutrition and healthcare, which delays menopause. No plausible direct causal path from menopause timing to economic output.

correlations.template: Countries with later menopause ({high_val} in {high_country}) tend to be happier ({high_outcome}). Countries with earlier menopause ({low_val} in {low_country}) less so ({low_outcome}). Menopause timing is a marker of overall development, not a driver of happiness.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ more happiness (development drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Menopause age is a proxy for nutritional and healthcare quality. The same conditions that produce later menopause produce happier societies. No direct causal link.

correlations.template: Later menopause and longer life go together, {high_val}/{high_outcome} in {high_country} vs {low_val}/{low_outcome} in {low_country}. Both are outputs of the same healthcare system.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ longer life (healthcare drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Shared driver: healthcare and nutrition quality affect both reproductive longevity and overall longevity.

correlations.template: Where menopause comes later ({high_val} in {high_country}), maternal mortality is lower ({high_outcome}). Where it comes earlier ({low_val} in {low_country}), mortality is higher ({low_outcome}). Both reflect the quality of a country's healthcare for women.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ fewer maternal deaths (healthcare drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause: healthcare quality for women affects both reproductive lifespan and maternal survival. No direct causal link between menopause timing and maternal mortality.

correlations.template: Later menopause ({high_val}) and lower inequality ({high_outcome}) in {high_country}. Earlier menopause ({low_val}) and higher inequality ({low_outcome}) in {low_country}. Both are markers of how much a society invests in women's wellbeing.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ more equality (investment in women drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause: societies that invest in women's health (delaying menopause) also invest in women's rights and economic participation.

correlations.template: Menopause at {high_val} and {high_outcome} healthy years in {high_country}. Menopause at {low_val} and {low_outcome} healthy years in {low_country}. Both track the same underlying health infrastructure.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ more healthy years (health systems drive both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause: overall health system quality and nutrition.

correlations.template: Countries with later menopause tend to have higher divorce rates, not because biology drives divorce, but because both correlate with women's economic independence and social freedom.
correlations.one_liner: Later menopause ↔ higher divorce (women's independence drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause: women's autonomy and economic independence allow both later menopause (better health) and higher divorce rates (freedom to leave unhappy marriages).

correlations.template: Where first births happen later ({high_val} in {high_country}), teen pregnancies are rare ({high_outcome} per 1,000). Where they happen earlier ({low_val} in {low_country}), teen pregnancies are common ({low_outcome}). Access to contraception, education, and family planning services drive both numbers.
correlations.one_liner: Later first birth → fewer teen pregnancies
correlations.mechanism: Nearly definitional but mediated by contraceptive access, sex education, and cultural norms around early childbearing.
correlations.improvement_path: To cut teen births: Delay first pregnancy → requires: sex education + contraceptive access + keeping girls in school → the three reinforce each other.

correlations.template: Later first births ({high_val} in {high_country}) correlate with more healthy years ({high_outcome}). Earlier first births ({low_val} in {low_country}) with fewer ({low_outcome}). Delaying childbirth reduces health risks, but healthier societies also enable delayed childbirth.
correlations.one_liner: Later first birth ↔ more healthy years
correlations.mechanism: Delayed childbirth reduces maternal health complications. But healthier societies also provide the contraception and economic conditions that enable delayed childbirth. N=8, interpret with caution.

correlations.template: First birth at {high_val} in {high_country}, life expectancy {high_outcome}. First birth at {low_val} in {low_country}, life expectancy {low_outcome}. Later first births and longer lives reinforce each other through better health systems.
correlations.one_liner: Later first birth ↔ longer life
correlations.mechanism: Similar to HALE: delayed childbirth reduces health risks, and societies with longer lifespans provide conditions for delayed childbirth. N=8.
correlations.improvement_path: To extend lives: Delay first birth → pregnancies are safer after age 25 + parents are more financially stable → better health outcomes for mother and child.

correlations.template: When women have their first child later ({high_val} in {high_country}), they tend to have fewer children total ({high_outcome}). In {low_country}, first birth at {low_val} and fertility rate {low_outcome}. The biological window narrows, and so do family size expectations.
correlations.one_liner: Later first birth → fewer children
correlations.mechanism: Direct biological and social mechanism: later first birth leaves fewer reproductive years and shifts social norms toward smaller families. The Korean compression is the extreme example.

correlations.template: This is the one milestone where 'later' means worse. In {low_country}, people buy their first home at {low_val} and happiness is {low_outcome}. In {high_country}, it's {high_val}, and happiness drops to {high_outcome}. Late home buying isn't a choice. It's a sign of unaffordable housing.
correlations.one_liner: Later home purchase → less happiness (unaffordability)
correlations.mechanism: Unlike other milestones, delayed home purchase reflects economic constraint, not opportunity. Housing unaffordability directly reduces life satisfaction and financial security.

correlations.one_liner: Likely artifact, driven by Japan outlier
correlations.mechanism: Japan has the latest home purchase age (38) and moderate GII. Denmark has the earliest (29.5) and lowest GII. With N=9, this is likely a Japan-driven artifact, not a real pattern.

correlations.template: Later cohabitation ({high_val} in {high_country}) and longer life ({high_outcome}) go together, but cohabitation age is estimated from surveys (low confidence data). Both reflect development level, not a direct connection.
correlations.one_liner: Later cohabitation ↔ longer life (development, but low confidence data)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause (development), but cohabitation data is survey-estimated and LOW confidence. Treat with caution. N=9.
correlations.improvement_path: To extend lifespan: Later cohabitation → reflects a society where people are educated longer, earn more, and access better healthcare before partnering.

correlations.template: Cohabitation timing and healthy lifespan correlate, but the cohabitation data is estimated, not measured. Both are likely driven by overall development level.
correlations.one_liner: Later cohabitation ↔ more healthy years (low confidence data)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause. Cohabitation data is LOW confidence. N=9.

correlations.template: Where people start living together later ({high_val} in {high_country}), teen pregnancies are rarer ({high_outcome}). Earlier cohabitation ({low_val} in {low_country}) correlates with more ({low_outcome}). Early partnership formation leads to earlier sexual activity and pregnancy.
correlations.one_liner: Earlier cohabitation → more teen pregnancies
correlations.mechanism: Plausible causal path: earlier partnership formation → earlier sexual activity → more adolescent pregnancies. But cohabitation data is LOW confidence.

correlations.template: Later cohabitation and lower gender inequality go together, both reflect societies where women have more autonomy and freedom to delay partnership.
correlations.one_liner: Later cohabitation ↔ more equality (women's autonomy drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause: women's autonomy. Cohabitation data is LOW confidence. N=9.
correlations.improvement_path: To reduce inequality: When cohabitation is delayed → it means women have more pre-partnership independence → which itself reduces structural gender gaps.

correlations.template: Later cohabitation compresses the reproductive window, leading to fewer children. {high_country} cohabits at {high_val} with fertility {high_outcome}. {low_country} at {low_val} with {low_outcome}.
correlations.one_liner: Later cohabitation → fewer children
correlations.mechanism: Similar to marriage: later partnership formation leaves less time for childbearing. But cohabitation data is LOW confidence.

correlations.template: Later cohabitation and lower maternal mortality both reflect better healthcare and more development. Not directly connected.
correlations.one_liner: Later cohabitation ↔ fewer maternal deaths (development drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause. Cohabitation data is LOW confidence. N=9.

correlations.template: Earlier menarche ({low_val} in {low_country}, happiness {low_outcome}) and later menarche ({high_val} in {high_country}, happiness {high_outcome}), but the connection is indirect. Earlier menarche reflects better childhood nutrition, which reflects national development, which drives happiness.
correlations.one_liner: Earlier menarche ↔ more happiness (nutrition/development drives both)
correlations.mechanism: Common cause: better childhood nutrition triggers earlier puberty AND is a marker of national development (which drives happiness). The negative r means later menarche (poorer nutrition) correlates with less happiness.

correlations.one_liner: Likely artifact, Korea/Japan effect with N=8
correlations.mechanism: Counterintuitive: later first births correlate with LOWER GDP. Driven by Korea and Japan having extremely late first births but not the highest GDPs. With N=8, this is too noisy to interpret reliably.

correlations.template: Later first births ({high_val} in {high_country}) mean fewer maternal deaths ({high_outcome}). Earlier first births ({low_val} in {low_country}) mean more ({low_outcome}). Pregnancies after 25 are medically safer than teen pregnancies.
correlations.one_liner: Later first birth → fewer maternal deaths
correlations.mechanism: Direct: delayed first birth reduces high-risk early pregnancies. Also correlates with better prenatal care access. N=8.

correlations.template: Countries with later first births tend to have fewer years in poor health, but with only 8 data points, this pattern is suggestive, not conclusive.
correlations.one_liner: Later first birth → fewer unhealthy years (suggestive)
correlations.mechanism: Plausible but N=8. Later first birth reduces maternal health complications and may correlate with better lifetime health management.

correlations.one_liner: Likely artifact, N=8, mixed directions
correlations.mechanism: Counterintuitive direction and small sample. Not reliable enough to present.
